constantly monitor own thoughts for signs of going crazy
try hard not think about the trauma

Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it
I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me

Memory.value: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt
I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.
My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed.

I have lost my connection to my community and culture

issues.explanation: Funerals, cemeteries, or grief-related events are not well linked to the stated trauma of witnessing childhood domestic violence, especially when the other trigger items center on male presence and shouting. This trigger is not impossible, but in this profile it stands out as insufficiently connected to the rest of the formulation.

Listening for signs that someone is entering the home suggests a burglary/home-intrusion threat theme, which is weakly connected to the selected trauma-specific cues and memory/appraisal content centered on domestic violence. It pulls the threat profile toward external break-in danger rather than reenacted interpersonal violence.

Noticing weapons or dangerous objects in any environment implies a generalized weapon-attack threat theme, but the trauma type and the rest of the items do not support a weapon-focused formulation. This makes the threat node less coherent with the memory and appraisal content.

'I have failed in my most important role in life' is a broad role-failure appraisal that is not clearly anchored to the selected trauma memories or other appraisals. The other negative appraisals emphasize weakness and disconnection; this item introduces a different theme without enough support elsewhere in the profile.

Drug use is not well supported by the rest of the five-component profile. The strongest formulation link is Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies, and the other strategies clearly fit trigger-driven internal threat management, whereas drug use introduces a more severe coping pattern without corresponding support from the other selected items.

vignette:
Rodrigo is a 64-year-old divorced Latin American man who works alone at a small jewelry repair bench in a strip mall in the outer suburbs of Houston. He came to his first intake appointment wearing a collared shirt buttoned to the throat, sitting with his back to the wall and his eyes moving steadily around the room. He spoke carefully, in measured sentences, as though each word had been inspected before release.

The events Rodrigo carries began before he had language for them. Growing up in a small household in San Antonio, he watched his father beat his mother across a span of years that felt, in memory, like a single unbroken night. What he remembers most precisely are not the long stretches of dread but the moments themselves: his father's face when his voice first rose, the particular sound a kitchen chair makes when it is thrown against linoleum, the shadow of a man's arm raised in a narrow hallway. These images are fixed and photographic - each one a still frame rather than a scene - and they remain, more than five decades later, with the clarity of something that happened this morning. The memories carry with them an immediate and crushing guilt. He had been the eldest child. He had not stopped it. He had hidden.

That guilt has calcified, over the decades, into a settled conviction: that he is a weak man who failed at the most fundamental thing a person can be asked to do, and that this failure placed him permanently outside the circle of his own community. He grew up in a culture where the protection of family was the measure of a man, and he had come to believe - quietly, without ever quite saying it aloud - that he had disqualified himself from that belonging long ago. This belief does not remain abstract. It surfaces most forcefully when the memories intrude, and the memories do not require much invitation. The sound of raised voices in the strip mall parking lot, a confrontation between customers at the counter next door, or simply finding himself alone in a room with another man - any of these can return him, without warning, to that hallway. When the triggers fire, the conviction of his own weakness arrives with them, and the shame of that conviction makes the memories feel even more present and inescapable, as though they are evidence he is compelled to keep reviewing.

His body has organized itself around the anticipation of danger in a way that has become indistinguishable from his ordinary attention. At his jeweler's bench, where he handles small tools all day, he is aware at every moment of what in his immediate environment could be used as a weapon - a loupe, a pair of pliers, the glass display case edge. He watches the few customers who enter with the focused assessment of someone who has learned that harm comes from people who appear ordinary. He cannot be told he is safe; the information does not reach whatever part of him is making that determination. This hypervigilance is itself a source of shame: a man who flinches at a raised voice, who scans a room like a frightened animal, is confirming everything he already believes about himself. And that belief - that he is weak, unmoored from his culture, a failed protector - keeps him primed, so that ordinary social friction reads as threat, and the threat keeps the memories close.

To manage all of this, Rodrigo has constructed a life of careful suppression. He tries, with considerable effort, not to think about his childhood, but the effort of not thinking has made the memories more intrusive, not less, and has kept them from ever settling into something integrated or distant. He monitors his own thoughts with the vigilance of a man watching for symptoms of a disease, frightened that if he lets his guard down he will lose his mind entirely. He does not allow himself to rest - relaxation feels like an open door - and this chronic tension has left him exhausted in a way that has slowly narrowed his world. He no longer attends the community events he once found meaningful. His divorce, several years ago, removed the last daily relationship that had given him structure. He has few friends now, and he does not pursue them.

What finally brought Rodrigo to seek help was a moment at his workbench three months ago when a delivery man raised his voice on a phone call just outside the shop door, and Rodrigo found himself crouched behind the counter, heart hammering, before he had any conscious awareness of moving. He sat on the floor for several minutes, and what he felt most was not fear but a profound and exhausted grief. He is not sure what he hopes for. What he is most afraid of is that there is nothing left to recover - that the boy who hid in the hallway is all he has ever been.
